title: Cloud-seeding permits: four Indonesian bodies give different answers
commitment: On 24 August, Malaysia's Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Arthur Joseph Kurup phoned Indonesian Environment Minister Jumhur Hidayat and said Malaysia was ready to help put out fires, including by cloud seeding in Indonesian airspace over shared border locations. On 25 August Jumhur welcomed the request and said his ministry had no objection in principle, with technical permits to be handled through the military (TNI) commander.
outcome: The TNI spokesperson said on 25 August that permits for these operations do not fall under the military, and that authority sits with the Transportation Ministry because the aircraft are not military planes. The meteorology agency BMKG, which oversees weather modification, said it had issued no permit or approval for Malaysian operations in Indonesian territory. The Transportation Ministry's civil aviation director general said no flight clearance request for Malaysian waterbombing aircraft had been received and that any application would be processed under the applicable regulations. The Foreign Ministry said it was still coordinating internally. The Star reports Malaysian officials thanked Jakarta for permitting the operations; The Jakarta Post reports that Indonesian agencies did not confirm a permit. The sources do not show whether Malaysian operations began.

officialResponse.summary: Environment Minister Jumhur Hidayat called the operations a mutually beneficial effort to reduce transboundary haze and said his ministry had coordinated with the TNI commander on technical permits.

title: President orders investigation of companies: suspects named by police
commitment: President Prabowo Subianto, during visits to Central Kalimantan (Saturday 22 August) and to Riau and South Sumatra (Monday 24 August), ordered law enforcement to investigate companies suspected of involvement in forest and land fires.
outcome: By 27 August the National Police (Bareskrim) had named 72 individuals as suspects in nine Sumatra and Kalimantan provinces for allegedly burning land to clear it for oil palm. The Forestry Ministry had imposed administrative penalties on six companies on 25 August. On 11 October the New Straits Times, citing the Indonesian Consul-General in Johor Baru, reported 97 police reports involving corporations and 46 suspects including five companies. The two police counts differ in scope and date and the sources do not reconcile them.

title: 42 concessions flagged for fire potential, 19 under field verification
commitment: The Environment Ministry's Deputy for Environmental Law Enforcement, Rizal Irawan, said at an online press conference on 31 August that strict liability applies when a fire occurs inside a concession, whether it was set deliberately or not. He said the ministry had flagged 42 companies for possible action over fires within their concession areas.
outcome: Nineteen of the 42 were undergoing field verification, with the rest to be inspected in a second stage. The company names were not released. On 11 October the New Straits Times reported that Indonesian authorities had still not disclosed the identities or nationalities of the 19 companies.

title: Environment Ministry opens enforcement against 21 companies
commitment: The Environment Ministry had sent preventative notices to 2,226 companies nationwide asking landholders to prepare firefighting staff, infrastructure and mitigation plans. On 2 September Rizal Irawan said the ministry had begun law enforcement against 21 companies, with field verification and monitoring signs placed at their sites.
outcome: The 21 companies hold land where over 11,400 hectares burned across seven provinces in Kalimantan and Sumatra (South Kalimantan 4 companies, West Kalimantan 7, South Sumatra 4, Central Kalimantan 3, Lampung 1, Riau 1, East Kalimantan 1). On 16 September Deputy Environment Minister Diaz Hendropriyono said about 50 companies across eight provinces had been sealed off, and that sanctions would apply if involvement in the fires is proven. The Antara report describes field verification and monitoring signs and does not mention penalties.

officialResponse.summary: Rizal Irawan: 'All 21 business entities are currently undergoing field verification.'

title: Forestry Ministry announces non-discriminatory enforcement; sanctions on 26 companies
commitment: On 23 September Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni announced the cancellation of business licences of five companies holding a combined 92,464 hectares of concessions in Kalimantan, where 1,169.13 hectares were affected by fire. He said the action follows President Prabowo's directive for 'law enforcement without discrimination, action that is not only directed at small players'.
outcome: On 11 October the New Straits Times reported that the Forestry Ministry had imposed administrative sanctions on 26 companies: five permits revoked, 13 suspended, and eight given written warnings or restoration orders. The New Straits Times figure is the one this site uses; the Forestry Ministry's own count was not available to us.

title: Indonesia says it has received no formal protest
commitment: Foreign Ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said on 17 September: 'We have not received any letter of protest from countries in the region or our neighbours.' Spokesperson Vahd Nabyl A Mulachela said the lack of a formal complaint does not mean Indonesia is ignoring the haze, and that Indonesia is following ASEAN haze response mechanisms including daily hotspot reporting and firefighting measures.
outcome: ASEAN had activated a Level 3 alert for severe transboundary haze on 26 August. Malaysia said it was ready to help and that Indonesia had not responded to the offer. On 15 October Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said Malaysia had not reached the stage of a diplomatic note or legal action and that a note is a last resort, so no formal protest had been sent as of that date.

officialResponse.summary: Foreign Ministry spokespeople said Indonesia is coordinating, holding dialogues and communicating with neighbours.

title: Top forestry concessions by hotspots: permits intact for three, frozen or revoked for six of ten
commitment: The Forestry Ministry announced permit revocations and suspensions for companies with fires on their concessions (see the Forestry Ministry sanctions entry).
outcome: Trend Asia's report 'Smoke for the People, Profit for the Few' (media briefing 6 October, page dated 7 October) states that the top three forestry concessions by 2026 hotspots, accounting for 275 hotspots, retain intact permits, and that six of the top ten have had permits frozen or revoked by authorities. It states that 15% of 34,933 high-confidence hotspots analysed (January 2024 to August 2026), or 5,082, fell in forestry concessions. The page does not give the status of the other four and quotes no government response. A hotspot inside a concession does not establish who lit the fire.

title: Aerial firefighting and cloud seeding grounded by visibility
commitment: By 26 August the disaster agency BNPB had deployed 52 aircraft, including 37 helicopters, across six provinces. On 12 October Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir told Malaysia's foreign minister that Indonesia has 34 aeroplanes and 34 helicopters, and that Indonesia had deployed 60,000 people on the ground.
outcome: On 12 October Mohamad Hasan quoted the Indonesian side as saying the aircraft cannot take off because 'visibility is so poor that it is unsafe for any flights in the affected areas', and that cloud seeding was not possible without suitable cumulonimbus clouds. On 14 October The Star reported that dense haze had blocked water-bombing and cloud-seeding flights in Central Kalimantan for more than a week, with ground crews doing the work. Aircraft counts differ between the August and October reports.

title: President says 'it really comes down to rain'; national disaster not declared
commitment: At a cabinet meeting on 12 October President Prabowo Subianto pledged 200 portable water pumps and 2 billion rupiah (about US$118,000) to drill at 200 locations around Tanjung Puting National Park, where more than 500 hectares were burning and visibility had fallen to about 500 metres.
outcome: In a video of the meeting posted on YouTube, Prabowo is quoted as saying: 'In the end, it really comes down to rain.' The Star reports he indicated rain may be the only way to clear the smog and allow aerial operations to resume. Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs Dudung Abdurachman ruled out declaring a national disaster, said the government can handle the crisis, and said foreign aid offers were not discussed at the meeting. Authorities expected rain from mid-October.

officialResponse.summary: Dudung Abdurachman said the government can handle the crisis without a national disaster declaration.

title: ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution and Malaysia's push for new mechanisms
commitment: Indonesia ratified the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution in 2014, according to The Jakarta Post. Hikmahanto Juwana of the University of Indonesia is quoted there as saying that rejecting ASEAN assistance could violate the agreement.
outcome: On 12 October Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said Malaysia would raise haze at an ASEAN foreign ministers' meeting ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila in November, because haze 'is not included or classified as a natural disaster' in existing ASEAN mechanisms. On 15 October he said Malaysia would submit a non-paper at the ASEAN Senior Officials' Meeting and Foreign Ministers' Meeting, preferred leader-level talks with Indonesia, and that Malaysia acknowledges Indonesia's efforts. The Star articles opened for this entry do not name the Agreement.

officialResponse.summary: Indonesia's Foreign Ministry said it follows ASEAN haze response mechanisms, including daily hotspot reporting and firefighting measures.
